Blood-stained: duct papilloma (most common), also intraductal carcinoma or duct ectasia. Serous: fibrocystic disease, duct ectasia, carcinoma. Black/green/paste-like (grumous): duct ectasia. What is ductography and how does its appearance distinguish the three main causes?

Contrast is injected into a major duct, then mammography is performed. It is indicated primarily for nipple discharge, especially blood-stained. Duct papilloma: small filling defect surrounded by contrast. Carcinoma: irregular mass or multiple intraluminal filling defects. Duct ectasia: dilated cystic structure. Mammography and cytology may also be done, but negative cytology never excludes cancer.

Microdochectomy vs radical duct excision — which is which?

Microdochectomy = excision of the single affected duct (via a lacrimal probe / stiff nylon and a periareolar or tennis-racquet incision); it is both the final diagnostic step and definitive treatment for localised discharge. Radical duct excision (Hadfield's operation) removes all major lactiferous ducts and is used for duct ectasia with multi-duct disease. Routine radical duct excision for localised discharge is NOT done.

Why is 'hyperestrogenemia' the common thread running through most breast cancer risk factors?

Early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity (peripheral aromatisation of androgens) and late first full-term pregnancy all increase lifetime exposure to oestrogen, which drives proliferation of breast epithelium. More dividing cells = more chances for a mutation to be fixed. Protective factors reverse this: prolonged breastfeeding and physical activity lower exposure.

Gail model versus Claus model — what does each use and what does each miss?

Gail: most frequently used; age at menarche, number of breast biopsies, age at first live birth, number of first-degree relatives with breast cancer; predicts cumulative risk by decade of life. Claus: based on prevalence of high-penetrance susceptibility genes; uses detailed family history (1st and 2nd degree relatives and their age at diagnosis), excludes other risk factors. Neither includes BRCA1/2 mutations, or rare/less consistent factors such as radiation, diet, OCP and lactation.

Describe the morphological progression of DCIS and its growth patterns.

Neoplastic proliferation of minor-duct epithelium: 1. Papillary growth into duct lumina. 2. Coalescence leaves rounded spaces → cribriform pattern. 3. Pleomorphic cells with mitoses obliterate lumina → solid pattern. 4. Cells outgrow blood supply → necrosis → comedo pattern. Classification is by nuclear grade and necrosis: low grade = cribriform, papillary, micropapillary; high grade = solid and comedocarcinoma. Calcification in necrotic areas explains its mammographic detection.

Why is LCIS considered a marker of risk rather than a true anatomic precursor?

LCIS arises in terminal duct lobular units, is usually multicentric and bilateral, and distorts them with cancer cells containing characteristic cytoplasmic mucoid globules. Invasive carcinoma develops in 25–35% of women with LCIS, but it occurs in EITHER breast and up to 65% of subsequent cancers are ductal, not lobular. That is why it is treated as a risk marker for the whole breast rather than a local precursor.

What clinical signs should make you suspect breast cancer, including locally advanced disease?

Change in breast size/shape, a hard lump, single-duct (especially blood-stained) discharge, nipple retraction, skin dimpling/puckering, axillary node enlargement. Advanced signs: peau-d'orange, skin ulceration, satellite nodules, and cancer en cuirasse (diffuse infiltration of breast skin and chest wall with nodules and ulceration). Peau-d'orange, dimpling/puckering and nipple retraction — what is the mechanism of each?

Dimpling/puckering: infiltration and shortening of Cooper's ligaments. Nipple retraction: fibrosis in and around the subareolar ducts. These are different anatomical clues, not interchangeable terms.

Define triple assessment and give its diagnostic performance.

Triple assessment = clinical examination + imaging (ultrasound or mammography) + tissue sampling (FNAC or core biopsy). A confident diagnosis is reached in 99.9% of cases when all three agree. First investigation for a suspected breast cancer is mammography; the definitive/best diagnostic investigation is biopsy.

Compare FNAC, core-cut biopsy and excisional biopsy for a breast lump.

FNAC: rapid, painless, cheap; needs an experienced cytopathologist; does not distinguish invasive from in-situ cancer; ER/PR/HER2 not routinely available; false negatives in fibrotic or well-differentiated tumours. Core-cut: gives histology readable by any pathologist; ER/PR/HER2 routinely available; preferred before neoadjuvant systemic therapy. Excision biopsy: rare false negatives, full histology, may be definitive lumpectomy; but costly, painful, leaves an incision and may be unnecessary for benign disease.

Give the key technical facts about mammography.

Uses bremsstrahlung X-rays; radiation dose 0.1 cGy per study (chest X-ray is 25% of this) with no demonstrated increase in breast cancer risk from screening doses. Two views: craniocaudal (better medial breast, more compression) and mediolateral oblique (images the greatest volume including upper outer quadrant and axillary tail of Spence). Used for screening asymptomatic women and to guide needle localisation/biopsy; sensitivity is reduced in young/dense breasts and it is inappropriate <35 years.

What characterises invasive ductal carcinoma (NST/scirrhous)?

Accounts for ~80% of breast cancers; presents as a solitary firm mass, usually in perimenopausal/postmenopausal women in the 5th–6th decades. Up to 60% have macroscopic or microscopic axillary node metastases at presentation. 'Scirrhous' reflects the dense desmoplastic fibrosis that produces the hard, fixed mass and skin retraction.

Compare the special histological subtypes of invasive breast cancer.

Medullary (4%): BRCA1-associated, soft/haemorrhagic, dense lymphoreticular infiltrate, large pleomorphic nuclei, sheet-like growth, better 5-year survival than NST. Mucinous/colloid (2%): elderly, bulky, extracellular pools of mucin, 33% node metastases, 5-yr survival 73%. Papillary (2%): 7th decade, small, papillae with fibrovascular stalks, low node metastasis rate. Tubular (2%): perimenopausal, distant metastases rare, long-term survival approaching 100% — best prognosis.

What is distinctive about invasive lobular carcinoma?

About 10% of breast cancers; frequently multifocal, multicentric and bilateral (hence often a contraindication to breast-conserving surgery). Tumour cells invade in single-file 'Indian file' strands and show cytoplasmic mucoid globules. It has a different metastatic pattern — peritoneal and meningeal involvement, less lung or bone metastasis — and is harder to detect on mammography.

Either mastectomy + axillary node status assessment, OR breast-conserving therapy + axillary assessment + radiotherapy. Adjuvant chemotherapy indications: node positive, tumour >1 cm, or node-negative >0.5 cm with adverse features (vascular invasion, high grade, HER2 overexpression, negative hormone receptors). How did adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer evolve in this chapter?

CMF (cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil) for 6 months reduced relapse risk ~25% over 10–15 years, but is no longer considered adequate. CAF added doxorubicin (Adriamycin). Modern regimens use an anthracycline (doxorubicin/epirubicin) plus a taxane; in the US AC (Adriamycin + cyclophosphamide) or AC + taxane is common. Anthracycline combinations outperform no treatment, single agents and CMF. Hormone therapy is started after chemotherapy to reduce side-effects; the effects are additive.

What is the basis of the functional anatomical division of the liver?

Functional anatomy is based on Couinaud's division of the liver into eight (subsequently nine) functional segments, according to the distribution of portal venous branches and the location of hepatic veins in the parenchyma. Segment IX is a recent subdivision of segment I and describes the part lying posterior to segment VIII. The liver is divided into four portal sectors by the main branches of the portal vein — right lateral, right medial, left medial and left lateral. Three main hepatic veins lie between these sectors as intersectorial veins; these intersectoral planes are also called portal fissures (scissures). Each sector is subdivided into segments based on their supply by tertiary divisions of vascular biliary sheaths.

How does motility change through the course of SBO, and what are the fluid consequences?

Describe the normal embryological rotation and fixation of the midgut.

Rapid growth plus elongation of the midgut starting in the fifth week leads to herniation of midgut with superior mesenteric vessels as its stalk. The midgut undergoes 270-degree counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric vessels; this initial rotation results in the normal position of the DJ flexure in the left upper quadrant at the level of the gastric antrum. The DJ flexure is fixed to the posterior abdominal wall by the ligament of Treitz, so the third portion of the duodenum lies posterior to the SMA. In the 10th week the herniated intestinal loop begins to return to the abdominal cavity and the cecocolic loop undergoes another 270-degree counterclockwise rotation around the SMA, placing the cecum in the right lower quadrant. The ascending and descending colon then become fixed. During weeks 4–5 the small intestine mesentery attaches to the posterior abdominal wall in a broad base extending diagonally from the DJ flexure to the cecum.

2. Choose the enteral access by site and aspiration risk: nasojejunal over nasogastric, jejunostomy over gastrostomy, and PEG for longer-term gastric feeding.
3. When the gut cannot be used, select TPN access by duration — peripheral feeding for up to 2 weeks, central venous access with the order subclavian > internal jugular > femoral, and Hickman lines for long-term use.
4. Match the formulation to the calorie mix and watch for catheter sepsis, pneumothorax, overfeeding and electrolyte disturbances.
5. In malnourished patients start feeding slowly with thiamine to avoid refeeding syndrome, and use CVP/PCWP to interpret fluid status and shock.

Give the chapter's central decision threads in one sequence.

1. Recognise shock as inadequate tissue perfusion and the MC cause of death among surgical patients.
2. Classify immediately — hypovolemic (MC), traumatic, cardiogenic, septic (hyperdynamic early, hypodynamic late), neurogenic, hypoadrenal — because treatment follows the class.

Define a sarcomere and its bands.

The H-zone (heller) is a paler region of the A-band containing thick filaments not superimposed by thin filaments. The M-line (Mittelscheibe) is a thin line within the H-zone formed of cross-connecting cytoskeletal elements.

What are the central decision threads for localising neuroanatomical lesions?

It is a lower motor neuron facial nerve lesion causing flaccid paralysis of ipsilateral muscles of facial expression: no forehead wrinkles, drooping eyebrow, inability to close/blink the eye, sagging mouth corner and inability to smile, whistle or blow. Describe the ovary, its attachments and microscopic structure.

The ovaries are the female gonads located in the pelvic cavity posterior to the broad ligament, in the ovarian fossa of Waldeyer between the divergent external and internal iliac vessels. Classical cytotoxics are divided into CCNS alkylating agents (nitrogen mustards, ethylenimines, alkyl sulfonates, nitrosoureas, triazines) and platinum compounds, and CCS antimetabolites (folic acid, purine and pyrimidine analogs), spindle poisons (vinca alkaloids and taxanes), topoisomerase inhibitors (epipodophyllotoxins and camptothecins) and antitumor antibiotics (anthracyclines, dactinomycin, bleomycin, mitomycin C). Hormonal agents (antiestrogens, antiandrogens, GnRH analogs, aromatase inhibitors, progestins, glucocorticoids) and miscellaneous agents (hydroxyurea, mitotane, L-asparaginase, retinoids, arsenic trioxide, pentostatin, biological response modifiers) act by noncytotoxic mechanisms. Modern targeted therapy adds monoclonal antibodies and small molecule inhibitors that act on defined molecular targets such as HER2, EGFR, VEGF, BCR-ABL and proteasomes.

Explain the mechanism of activation and action of isoniazid.

Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase encoded by KatG. The active metabolite inhibits ketoenoylreductase (encoded by inhA), which is required for mycolic acid synthesis — an essential component of the mycobacterial cell wall. It acts through an oxygen-dependent pathway (catalase-oxidase reaction). It is bacteriostatic against resting organisms and bactericidal against rapidly multiplying bacilli; it is effective both intracellularly and extracellularly. KatG mutation causes high-level resistance; inhA mutation confers cross-resistance to ethionamide. Strains are presumed susceptible when resistance is below 4%.

Describe the mechanism, spectrum and distribution of rifampicin.

Rifampicin is a derivative of rifamycin (other derivatives: rifabutin, rifapentine). It is bactericidal against both dividing and non-dividing mycobacteria and acts by inhibiting DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. It penetrates all membranes, including the blood-brain and placental barriers, and is equally effective against intra- and extracellular bacilli. It is the only bactericidal drug active against dormant bacteria in solid caseous lesions.

Outline the pharmacokinetics and clinically important drug interactions of rifampicin.

Undergoes enterohepatic circulation and is partly metabolised in the liver; coloured metabolites cause orange discolouration of urine and secretions and staining of contact lenses. Eliminated mainly in the faeces, so it can be used safely in renal dysfunction. Food interferes with absorption — give on an empty stomach. A potent inducer of drug-metabolising enzymes: increases metabolism of anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives, oral anticoagulants and antiretroviral drugs. Women on oral contraceptives should increase the pill dose or use another method; patients on warfarin should be switched to unfractionated heparin or a low-molecular-weight heparin. PAS delays its absorption, so concomitant administration should be avoided.

Parasites then enter red cells (erythrocytic stage), which causes the symptoms of fever, chills and rigors; drugs acting here give clinical cure and suppressive prophylaxis. Some schizonts remain dormant in the liver (exo-erythrocytic/hypnozoite stage), causing relapse; drugs acting here give radical cure. Gametes in blood are taken up by the mosquito (transmission); gametocidal drugs prevent transmission. The exo-erythrocytic stage is absent in P. falciparum, so relapses do not occur.

Describe the RER branch, the signal peptide hypothesis and the properties of signal peptides.

Proteins synthesized on membrane-bound polyribosomes contain a signal peptide that mediates their attachment to the ER membrane. The signal peptide hypothesis, proposed by Blobel and Sabatini, explains the distinction between free and membrane-bound polyribosomes: proteins synthesized on membrane-bound polyribosomes have an N-terminal peptide extension (signal peptide) that attaches them to ER membranes and facilitates transfer into the ER lumen, after which they are sorted to various membranes and lysosomes. Certain ER membrane proteins are transferred directly into the ER membrane without reaching the lumen. Proteins made on free ribosomes are targeted to mitochondria, nuclei, peroxisomes and cytosol, while RER-synthesized proteins are destined for the ER membrane, Golgi membrane and plasma membrane; an exception is that lysosomal proteins are also synthesized in the RER branch. List the five steps of cotranslational translocation of proteins into the ER lumen.

Step 1: the signal sequence emerges from the ribosome and binds SRP, temporarily arresting further elongation. Step 2: the SRP-ribosome-nascent protein complex binds the SRP receptor; SRP guides the protein to SRP-R. Step 3: SRP is released from SRP-R, the ribosome binds the translocon (Sec61 complex), the signal peptide inserts into the channel and translation resumes; SRP and SRP-R bind GTP and, when they interact, GTP is hydrolysed and SRP dissociates. Step 4: the signal peptide opens the translocon channel by binding hydrophobic residues, moving the plug; the channel opens only when signal peptide is present. Step 5: the signal peptide is cleaved by signal peptidase and the fully translocated protein is released into the ER lumen.

Proteins are polymers of amino acids containing carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen; nitrogen is characteristic and averages 16% by weight. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds formed between the alpha-carboxyl group of one amino acid and the alpha-amino group of another, creating a rigid, planar, polar but uncharged CO-NH bridge with partial double-bond character and a trans C-N bond. The free amino end is the N-terminus and the free carboxyl end is the C-terminus, and sequences are written N-terminal to C-terminal. Atypical isopeptide bonds involve a non-alpha group, occur post-translationally and are protease resistant.

Summarize the chapter: how do the TCA cycle, shuttles, ETC, ATP synthase and inhibitors fit together?

The TCA cycle in mitochondria oxidizes acetyl-CoA to CO2, producing 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP/GTP per turn (10 ATP). Cytosolic NADH reaches the mitochondria through glycerophosphate, malate or creatine phosphate shuttles. NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the four ETC complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane; electrons flow in ascending order of redox potential to oxygen. Proton pumping generates a proton motive force; protons re-enter through ATP synthase (F0 proton channel, F1 catalytic head) to make ATP by the binding change mechanism. Electron transfer, oxidative phosphorylation, uncoupling and ionophores are all targets of specific inhibitors. High energy compounds such as ATP, phosphocreatine and phosphoenolpyruvate store the energy captured by these pathways.

What should be known about metabolic acidosis, illicit liquor and ocular toxicity in methanol poisoning?

Muscle fibres contain myofibrils with actin and myosin filaments. At rest, actin interdigitates myosin slightly and muscle is soft and supple, maintained by adequate ATP. Define mummification and list its salient features.

Mummification is rapid dehydration/desiccation and shriveling of the dead body from evaporation of water, with preservation of natural appearances and features - a dry decomposition modifying putrefaction. It depends on the fact that no two people have exactly the same DNA sequence and, although only limited segments are scrutinized, those segments are statistically unique. It is rapidly becoming the primary method for identifying and distinguishing human beings.

Summarise the comments on the legal test of insanity.

The insanity must be directly related to the offence so that the mental abnormality had a direct causative relationship and the offence would not have occurred without it. 'Abnormality of the mind' is any disease capable of producing mental dysfunction; the law is concerned with the mind (reason, memory and understanding) rather than the brain. Mental dysfunction attributable to voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs is not abnormality of the mind, which usually means a major functional or organic psychosis. It must be clearly established that reasoning powers were not functioning normally due to a defect in intellectual and cognitive faculties. The rule concerns the ability to distinguish right from wrong with reference to the particular crime: if the accused had capacity to know his act was wrong he is fully responsible even if mentally ill and unable to refrain; a person committing a crime under an insane delusion is judged as though the delusional facts were real.

Summarise the forensic psychiatric approach to mental disorder and responsibility.

Forensic psychiatry applies psychiatric knowledge to the administration of justice. Symptoms such as delusion, hallucination, illusion, impulse and obsession must be distinguished, and the mental status examination with assessment of insight and judgment is central. There is transmural inflammation (full thickness), which causes weakness leading to fissure and fistula formation; fibrosis is common and perianal fistula is the most common fistula. There is patchy involvement ('skip lesions') with normal intervening mucosa, producing cobblestone mucosa. Non-caseating granulomas are present.

Give a high-yield synthesis of the key facts covered in this DNB orthopaedics summary.

Tumours: Maffucci = enchondromas + hemangiomas; chondroblastoma is epiphyseal before maturity; osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant tumour except myeloma; myeloma is the commonest primary bone malignancy; Ewing's arises in the medullary cavity; prostate gives osteoblastic metastases; Enneking staging. Infections: Staphylococcus aureus is commonest; TB spine is thoracic; Salmonella in sickle cell disease; sequestrum = chronic; Brodie's abscess = subacute. Fractures: Colles in elderly women; cubitus varus after supracondylar fracture; FLUTS non-union sites; Monteggia and Galeazzi fracture-dislocations. Pediatric: CTEV and Ponseti; DDH, Barlow and Ortolani; Perthes 4–8 years with MRI; SCFE and Trethowan; Blount and Siffert-Katz; congenital pseudoarthrosis of tibia. Arthritis: OA DIP/PIP/1st CMC sparing MCP and wrist; RA PIP/MCP/wrist sparing DIP; swan neck; HLA-B27 and bamboo spine; gout 1st MTP with negative birefringence; pseudogout knee with positive birefringence; Charcot from diabetes. Nerves: Erb C5–C6, Klumpke C8–T1; radial best and sciatic worst prognosis; axillary in shoulder dislocation and surgical neck; radial in shaft; ulnar in medial epicondyle; tardy ulnar after lateral condyle; carpal and tarsal tunnel compressions. Metabolic: rickets, osteomalacia, osteoporosis; hyperparathyroidism, Paget, osteopetrosis, osteogenesis imperfecta, fluorosis. Sports: O'Donoghue triad; Lachman, drawer and McMurray tests; ATFL in ankle sprain. General: clavicle first to ossify; talus no muscles; iliofemoral ligament; joint classifications; Thomas, Trendelenburg and Ober tests.

Describe the basic steps of FESS using Messerklinger's technique.

What are the features of recurrent cervical cancer and how is local pelvic recurrence managed?

Recurrence may occur locally in the pelvis or para-aortic region, as distant metastases, or as a combination. The pelvis is the most common site of recurrence, and patients with only locally recurrent disease after definitive therapy are in a more favourable, potentially curable situation. Good prognostic factors are an isolated central pelvic recurrence without pelvic sidewall involvement, a long disease-free interval and a recurrent tumour less than 3 cm in diameter. Pelvic relapse after primary surgery may be treated by radical chemoradiation or pelvic exenteration. Confirmation by biopsy is essential before either therapy. The extent of disease and pelvic lymph node involvement are prognostic. Concurrent chemotherapy with cisplatin and/or 5-fluorouracil may improve outcome. Pelvic exenteration is feasible when there is no intraperitoneal or extrapelvic spread and a clear tumour-free space exists between recurrence and pelvic sidewall. A PET/CT scan is the most sensitive noninvasive test for distant disease and should be performed before exenteration if possible.

The fundus is palpated with both hands to identify the fetal pole (breech or head) occupying the uterine fundus. Describe the indications and procedure of external cephalic version.

Indications: breech presentation and transverse lie. Procedure: the maneuver is carried out on or after 37 weeks under the effect of terbutaline 0.25 mg SC or isoxsuprine 50–100 µg IV. Ultrasound examination confirms the diagnosis and adequacy of amniotic fluid volume. A reactive NST should precede the maneuver. ECV is attempted and followed by a repeat NST after the procedure; a reactive NST should be obtained after completing the procedure. There may be undue bradycardia due to head compression, expected to settle by 10 minutes; if fetal bradycardia persists, keep in mind cord entanglement and do reversion. If version is successful the patient is observed for 30 minutes to allow the fetal heart rate to settle. If fetal distress persists even after reversion, cesarean should be done. Ref. Dutta Obs. 9/e, p 542.

Describe internal podalic version: prerequisites, contraindications and complications.

IPV: in modern obstetrics there is no place for this procedure in a singleton pregnancy; it is only used for the second twin lying transversely when external version fails. Prerequisites: membranes should be intact or very recently ruptured (liquor adequate); cervix fully dilated; fetus must be living. Anesthesia: general anesthesia (halothane). Contraindications: obstructed labor; membranes ruptured with all liquor drained; previous cesarean section even if LSCS; contracted pelvis. Compare constriction ring and retraction ring (Bandl ring): nature, cause, situation and uterine state.

Nature: constriction ring is a manifestation of localized incoordinate uterine contraction; retraction ring is the end result of tonic uterine contractions and retractions. Cause: undue irritability of the uterus versus following obstructed labor. Situation: usually at the junction of upper and lower segment but may occur elsewhere, with a fixed position once formed, versus always at that junction with a position that progressively moves upward. Uterus: in constriction ring the upper segment contracts and retracts with relaxation in between and the lower segment remains thick and loose; in retraction ring the upper segment is tonically contracted with no relaxation, the wall becomes thicker and the lower segment is distended and thinned out.

Compare constriction ring and retraction ring (Bandl ring): maternal condition, examination findings and end result.

Maternal condition: almost unaffected unless labor is prolonged versus features of maternal exhaustion and sepsis. Abdominal examination — constriction ring: uterus normal and nontender, fetal parts easily felt, ring not felt, round ligament not felt, FHS usually present. Retraction ring: uterus tense and tender, fetal parts not easily felt, ring felt as an obliquely placed groove, taut tender round ligaments felt, FHS usually absent. Vaginal examination — constriction ring: lower segment not pressed by presenting part, ring felt usually above the head, features of obstructed labor absent. Retraction ring: lower segment very much pressed, ring cannot be felt vaginally, features of obstructed labor present. Explain why the diagnosis in the 8-week gesture sac with absent fetal parts is incarcerated abortion.

Ectopic pregnancy is ruled out by amenorrhoea of 8 weeks and an intrauterine gestational sac. Threatened abortion is ruled out because ultrasound shows a gestational sac with absent fetal parts, whereas threatened abortion shows a well-formed gestational sac with central echoes from the embryo and fetal cardiac motion. Question 6. Arias stella reaction is not seen in: a) Ovarian pregnancy b) Molar pregnancy c) Interstitial pregnancy d) Salpingitis isthmica nodosa

Ans. d) Salpingitis isthmica nodosa. Ovarian and interstitial pregnancy are ectopic, and molar pregnancy causes blighting, so it may be seen in all three. Question 8. Diagnostic criteria for primary abdominal pregnancy: a) Spiegelberg criteria b) Rubin's criteria c) Studdiford criteria d) Wrigley criteria

Ans. c) Studdiford's criteria. Ref. Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 188. Ovarian pregnancy: Spiegelberg criteria — sac occupies the position of the ovary, connected to the uterus by the ovarian ligament, definite ovarian tissue in the sac wall. Cervical pregnancy: Rubin's (Palmaan's) criteria — uterus smaller than distended cervix, internal os not dilated, curettage nonproductive of placental tissue, external os opens earlier. Placenta previa: sudden painless recurrent bleeding, always revealed and bright red; pallor proportionate to loss; fundal height corresponds to gestation; soft relaxed uterus; fetal parts easily palpated; high floating head; malpresentations common, most commonly transverse lie; fetal heart sounds usually normal; normal incidence of preeclampsia; coagulopathy rare; no IUGR. Abruptio placenta: severe abdominal pain, revealed or concealed bleeding that may be out of proportion and darker in color; pallor may be out of proportion; fundal height increased in concealed variety; tense, tender and rigid uterus; fetal parts difficult to palpate; head usually fixed; malpresentations uncommon; distress or absent fetal heart sounds; increased preeclampsia; frequent coagulopathy; IUGR may be seen because of associated PIH.

Define vasa previa and list its risk factors.

Vasa previa is a condition in which fetal blood vessels unsupported by umbilical cord or placental tissue overlie the internal os and are vulnerable to rupture when the supporting membranes rupture. It results from velamentous insertion of the cord, where the cord is inserted onto the fetal membranes. Risk factors are bilobate or succenturiate placenta and placenta previa or low-lying placenta.

What does Fig. 18.6 of vasa previa teach as text?

It shows fetal vessels running within the membranes over the internal os, unsupported by Wharton jelly, as a result of velamentous cord insertion. These unprotected vessels are easily lacerated when the membranes rupture, producing fetal bleeding.

What happens when membranes rupture in vasa previa and how is it diagnosed and managed?

The velamentously inserted cord ruptures along with the membranes, causing fetal blood loss. Fetal mortality is 75 to 90% while maternal mortality is not increased. It can be diagnosed antenatally by Doppler study; when bleeding occurs a sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern is seen. Diagnosis at the time of bleeding is by the Singer alkali denaturation or Apt test. Management is emergency cesarean section.

Describe the principle and interpretation of the Apt test, the Singer alkali denaturation test.

Principle: fetal hemoglobin HbF resists acid and alkali denaturation whereas adult hemoglobin HbA is easily denatured. Take the blood coming from the mother's vagina in a test tube and add NaOH or KOH. If the blood remains red or pink it has not been denatured, so HbF is present, the blood is fetal and the condition is vasa previa; this is called a negative Apt test. If the blood turns yellow-brown, HbA has been denatured, so the blood is maternal and the condition is placenta previa; this is called a positive Apt test.

Compare the Apt test with the Kleihauer-Betke test.

Both rely on HbF resistance to alkali in the Apt test and to acid in the Kleihauer-Betke test, so maternal HbA containing red cells are hemolyzed but fetal HbF containing cells are not. Apt test: sample is vaginal discharge or blood, reagent is 1% NaOH, qualitative assessment, used to rule out vasa previa late in pregnancy and to detect whether neonatal blood in vomiting or hemoptysis is swallowed maternal blood. Kleihauer-Betke test: sample is maternal peripheral smear, reagent is citric acid phosphate buffer, quantitative assessment, used to estimate how much fetal blood has entered the maternal circulation to assess isoimmunization risk and hemolytic disease of the newborn; it is the test used to differentiate fetal red blood cells from maternal red blood cells.

What is monochorionic dizygotic twinning and how does blood chimerism occur?

Monochorionic diamniotic placenta is rare in dizygotic twins; all documented cases followed ovulation induction alone or during an IVF cycle. What additional facts should be known about the Kleihauer-Betke test?

The Kleihauer-Betke test is performed on maternal blood to assess the amount of fetomaternal bleed and calculate the required Anti D dose. Describe the NESTROFT procedure.

Naked Eye Single Tube Red Cell Osmotic Fragility Test: take 2 mL of 0.36% buffered saline in one tube and 2 mL of distilled water in another. Add a drop of blood to each tube and leave both undisturbed for 20 minutes. Shake the tubes and hold them against a white paper with a black line drawn on it. Normally the line is clearly visible through the distilled water tube. If the line is clearly visible through the buffered saline tube too, the test is negative; if it is not clearly visible, the test is positive.

Explain the answer to New Pattern Question 21: Prolactinoma Teaching.

N21. Ans. is b, i.e. Increase in prolactin levels means worse prognosis. Ref. Leon Speroff 8/e, p 481; Dewhurst’s Textbook of Obs. and Gynae. 7/e, p 255–256; Williams Obs. 23/e, p 1139–1140. Prolactinoma is a benign prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour, the most common type of primary tumour, more common in women. Microprolactinoma 10 mm. Endocrine effects: infertility, menstrual irregularity, decreased libido, galactorrhea; local mass effect: visual field defect. Treatment: asymptomatic — observation; symptomatic — dopamine agonists (initial therapy in all cases; DOC cabergoline followed by bromocriptine) or surgery for resistant/intolerant cases. In pregnancy the pituitary doubles in size and estrogen drives tumour growth: clinically significant growth is 1–2% for microadenomas and 15–20% for macroadenomas. Regular visual checkup is advised; macroadenoma >1 cm is associated with bad prognosis. Prolactin rises physiologically from 5–8 weeks (20–40 ng/mL end of first trimester, 50–150 second, 100–400 third), so the level does not indicate poor prognosis.

How does fetal immune capacity develop?

The active immunological capacity of the fetus and neonate is compromised compared with older children and adults. Fetal cell-mediated and humoral immunity begin to develop by 9 to 15 weeks' gestation. The primary fetal response to infection is immunoglobulin M (IgM); passive immunity is provided by IgG transferred across the placenta.

The drug of choice for treating a pregnant woman with chickenpox is acyclovir, used with caution before 20 weeks. Acyclovir is initiated within 24 hours of the onset of rash if the period of amenorrhoea is more than 20 weeks' gestation. When does congenital varicella syndrome occur and how is it excluded?

What is neonatal varicella and how does maternal antibody timing affect severity?

Neonatal varicella is characterised by pneumonitis, hepatitis and DIC. Its severity is inversely related to the concentration of maternal antibodies present in newborn circulation. The mother starts producing and transferring antibodies approximately 5 days after onset of her disease, so babies born 5 days or more from the beginning of maternal disease will be protected. Exposure just before or during delivery, before maternal antibody forms, carries attack rates of 25 to 50 percent and mortality approaching 30 percent; some neonates develop disseminated visceral and CNS disease, commonly fatal.

How should delivery be timed and how is the neonate protected in maternal varicella?

If there is no fetal or maternal risk, delivery should be delayed for at least 7 days after onset of rash to allow time for maternal seroconversion and passive antibody transfer to the fetus. Perinatal exposure just before or during delivery poses a serious threat, so VZIG should be given to all neonates born to mothers with clinical evidence of varicella 5 days before and up to 2 days after delivery. VZIG decreases the chances of neonatal varicella and modifies the clinical course but does not always prevent severe or fatal disease. Expectant treatment with close observation, followed by prompt antiviral therapy on suspicion of neonatal varicella, is recommended. How is CMV transmitted to the fetus and neonate?

Being a herpes virus, latent infection and reactivation can occur, especially in pregnancy. Fetal infection can follow primary maternal infection or reactivation, so previous infection does not prevent congenital infection. Describe the FDA pregnancy categories for drugs.

Category A: no fetal risk demonstrated by well-controlled human studies (e.g., penicillin, ampicillin). Category B: no risk in animal studies but no human studies, or adverse animal effects not confirmed in well-controlled human trials (e.g., paracetamol, ranitidine). Category C: no animal or human studies, or adverse fetal effects in animals only (e.g., chloroquine, acyclovir, zidovudine). Category D: proven risk but use is essential because benefits outweigh risks (e.g., phenytoin, warfarin, propylthiouracil). Category X: clearly teratogenic, risks outweigh benefits and the drug should be avoided (isotretinoin). Remember: isotretinoin causes CNS anomaly (NTD), CVS anomaly and facial defects.

Summarize asthma in pregnancy: effects, exacerbations, severity and management.

Asthma is the most common chronic condition in pregnancy, affecting 3–12% of gestations. Its course is unpredictable: 20% improve, 30% deteriorate and 50% remain unchanged; deterioration is more likely with severe asthma. Exacerbations are most frequent at 24–36 weeks, precipitated by viral respiratory infections and noncompliance with inhaled corticosteroids. Effects on pregnancy: preterm labor, PROM, preeclampsia, low birth weight and slight increase in abruptio placentae. Severity correlates with FEV1 and PEFR; FEV1 ideally above 80% of predicted. Management: mild asthma — inhaled beta agonist (albuterol preferred); mild persistent — low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (budesonide preferred); moderate — low-dose ICS plus long-acting beta agonist (salmeterol); severe — high-dose ICS plus LABA and oral steroids if needed. PGF-2 alpha is absolutely contraindicated in asthma: for PPH use PGE1, and for cervical ripening use PGE2.

Describe bacterial vaginosis and its diagnosis and treatment in pregnancy.
